title: POC Weekly: Latency Tuning - TTFT & Streaming

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-14 16:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Carlos Mendez (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood CSM), Michael Tan (AcmePay VP Eng), Sara Liu (ML Eng), David Cho (Infra)

[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is our weekly POC sync. Quick check — agenda is TTFT and streaming regressions, kernel bench follow-ups, and next steps. Carlos is going to lead on the perf stuff.
[00:18] Carlos Mendez: Yeah hi all, good to see you. Quick recap: last week we enabled streaming to get earlier tokens out for end user experience but we saw TTFT on average went down, but some cases TTFT increased for short prompts. I want to walk through what we measured and why.
[00:35] Michael Tan: Ok, yeah that spike on short prompts surprised us — users noticed a lag before first token. We're trying to keep median under 120ms TTFT.
[00:44] Carlos Mendez: Right, and just to be clear — when I say TTFT I mean time from request accepted by Redwood edge to first token emitted, not client rendering. We instrumented at the router and at the runtime.
[00:58] Sara Liu: There's some noise in our client telemetry too but we've isolated a pattern: short prefix prompts (~10-40 tokens) saw TTFT go up when streaming was enabled because the runtime waited to fill a small internal batch before flushing first token.
[01:18] Priya Singh: Is that the continuous batching policy? I remember there's a threshold.
[01:23] Carlos Mendez: Exactly. We have continuous batching with a time threshold and a token threshold. When streaming we're trying not to hurt throughput so the runtime sometimes holds a tiny bit to amortize kernel launch cost. For longer prompts or high QPS it's fine.
[01:39] David Cho: Are there kernel startup costs here? We run on mixed hardware and kernels matter.
[01:44] Carlos Mendez: Yes, kernel invocation and model forward latency per chunk. Also sequence length influences kernel selection — for small sequences some fused kernels are faster, for long sequences others are better. We saw cases where the runtime selected a kernel optimized for throughput that added latency for small batches.
[02:03] Michael Tan: Hmm, so it's kernel + batching policy interplay. Could we force a low-latency kernel for the first chunk?
[02:10] Carlos Mendez: We can. We have a canary config that forces a low-latency kernel on first token emission and then switch back. But you trade off throughput and unit cost.
[02:20] Sara Liu: Do we have numbers on cost tradeoff? If we force low-latency kernels across the board, are we looking at 20%+ cost increase?
[02:29] Carlos Mendez: Ballpark yes, depends on QPS and prompt length distribution. For AcmePay's mix — based on last week's logs — about 12-18% increase if applied globally. But if we do a routing rule for short-prompts only, the impact is much smaller.
[02:44] Lena Park: This matches our optimization thesis: targeted policies + caching/batching reduce unit cost impact.
[02:50] Michael Tan: Can you walk through the kernel choices you mentioned? We saw references to int8 kernels in the doc.
[02:56] Carlos Mendez: Sure. We tested fp16 fused matmul kernels vs int8 kernels (quantized). Int8 reduces per-token compute and memory, often improving throughput and cost, but sometimes int8 has slightly higher first-chunk overhead because of dequantization costs and different kernel launch patterns. For many of our test cases int8 improved end-to-end tail latency, but in a few short-prompt cases TTFT regressed by 30-50ms.
[03:24] Sara Liu: So int8 might help throughput but not always TTFT for short prompts. Is there a way to get the best of both?
[03:29] Carlos Mendez: We recommend hybrid: use int8 for steady-state tokens and a low-latency fp16 path for the first few tokens, or route short prompts to a low-latency pool. That is what we plan to bench next.
[03:41] David Cho: From infra side, how hard is it to maintain two pools? We're using dedicated capacity for the POC.
[03:47] Carlos Mendez: Not hard. Redwood Dedicated supports multiple pools and routing by policy. You can create a low-latency pool (smaller batch windows, different kernel selection) and a throughput pool. Router will send short prompt traffic to low-latency pool.
[03:58] Michael Tan: What about streaming chunk size? We noticed chunking at 32 tokens vs 64 made a difference.
[04:04] Carlos Mendez: Right — chunk size affects both TTFT and bandwidth. Smaller chunks mean earlier emission but more kernel calls. For your latency targets, 16-32 token chunk looks sweet for most. For very short prompts chunking sometimes didn't even happen, which exposed batching delay.
[04:20] Sara Liu: Can we reduce the batching time threshold? We previously set it to 10ms to hit throughput goals.
[04:25] Carlos Mendez: You can lower it to 3-5ms for short-prompt routing, but that again increases cost. It also increases tail variance under bursty traffic.
[04:35] Priya Singh: Quick question: did the streaming client library add any unintended backpressure? We saw some retry patterns.
[04:41] Michael Tan: We had one bug but it's fixed. The current behavior is fine.
[04:45] Carlos Mendez: Ok good. So actionable bench plan: run per-kernel TTFT and tail for seq lens 64, 512, 1024, 4096 with streaming enabled and disabled, and with fp16 vs int8. We'll measure median, p95, p99 and cost per 1M tokens.
[05:05] Michael Tan: That sounds great. Can you also include a test with prefix caching enabled? Our use has a lot of template prefix reuse.
[05:12] Carlos Mendez: Yes — prefix caching/kv cache reduces compute for repeated prefixes — that tends to help TTFT for repeated work because cached KV avoids full forward on the prefix. We'll include cache and no-cache runs.
[05:22] Sara Liu: For the seq-length histogram — we'll export our production distribution and send it. Most of our calls are short, around 24-80 tokens, but we have long tails up to 3k.
[05:33] Lena Park: Perfect, that validates routing short prompts to low-latency pool.
[05:38] David Cho: Any security or network concerns when we run these tests on dedicated? We need to keep the VPC private and KMS in our control.
[05:45] Carlos Mendez: For Dedicated the control plane still manages routing but data path stays in your VPC, and we respect customer KMS/EKM for keys. No data leaves your network in this POC. We'll include logs only with consent.
[05:58] Michael Tan: Competitors — Anthropic did publish some perf notes, but we still want to see Redwood's kernel breakdowns.
[06:05] Carlos Mendez: We'll add competitor baseline columns where we can.
[06:08] Priya Singh: Quick admin — Lena will update the perf spreadsheet and Carlos will run bench and share raw CSVs.
[06:15] Lena Park: Yup, I'll share by Friday.
[06:17] Carlos Mendez: Ok I want to call out an oddity: for one test the runtime selected a fused attention kernel that is faster for long sequences, but due to a heuristic it was chosen for medium sequences and that increased first-chunk latency. We're going to tweak the heuristic in the bench harness to force per-seq-length selection.
[06:36] Sara Liu: Is that a runtime change or just a config toggle?
[06:40] Carlos Mendez: Mostly config/runtime flag — no model code changes. We'll run canary on a test pool.
[06:46] Michael Tan: If we implement the per-seq heuristic, what's the rollout risk? We can't have regressions to tail latency in production.
[06:53] Carlos Mendez: We'll do canary and A/B — route 5% of traffic to new heuristic and monitor p99. If p99 stays within SLO we ramp. We can also auto-fallback.
[07:04] David Cho: That sounds fine. We'll want audit logs and an easy rollback.
[07:09] Carlos Mendez: Audit logs are automatic for Dedicated and we can expose them.
[07:12] Lena Park: Any more questions?
[07:14] Michael Tan: One more — do you have guidance on streaming client buffer sizes? We saw front-end jitter when we pushed smaller chunks.
[07:21] Carlos Mendez: For web clients, buffering at client and server needs coordination; we recommend a 50-100ms client-side buffer to avoid rendering micro-jitters. We'll add a note to the doc.
[07:31] Sara Liu: Great.
[07:33] Lena Park: Ok quick recap of next steps: Lena shares perf spreadsheet, Carlos runs bench (fp16 vs int8, streaming on/off, cache on/off) across seq lens and shares raw CSVs, AcmePay shares seq-length histogram and example prefixes, David toggles extra first-byte logging. We'll aim to reconvene after bench results.
[07:51] Michael Tan: Thanks everyone, appreciate the focused plan.
[07:54] Priya Singh: Thanks all, we'll follow up in Slack with links.
[07:58] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional filler and slight mis-hears (e.g., "KV cash" instead of "KV cache") preserved.
